title: When it rains
tomorrow: a friend is in the hospital. what do you actually say?

cards: Here's a strange pair of requests, both in the hadith collection of al-Bukhari, both made during Friday sermons, one Friday apart. First, a man stands up while the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is preaching.
The animals are dying, the roads are cut, he says. Pray for rain. The Prophet raises his hands and prays, and the rain comes, and keeps coming until the next Friday.
Then a man stands up again. Now the houses are falling and the roads are cut. Pray for it to stop.
Same sky. Same water. Opposite prayers.

teach.b: Both, and the second answer is the clue. The Prophet doesn't pray the rain away. He raises his hands and asks: around us, not on us.
On the hills, the valleys, the places where trees grow. The rain isn't canceled; it's moved to where it can help. Now the short line Muslims say when rain begins, also in al-Bukhari, makes sense.
It's two words in Arabic: sayyiban nafi'an. A pouring rain, a beneficial one. That second word does all the work.
Rain on its own isn't simply good or bad.
The same storm fills a farmer's well and floods a basement. So the prayer doesn't just ask for more of a thing. It asks for the kind that does good.
Then there's one more detail, from Sahih Muslim, the kind you'd tell a friend tonight. Once, when rain began, the Prophet pulled back part of his garment so the drops would land on him.
Asked why, he said, in effect: it has just come from its Lord.

He wanted to feel it fresh, the way a kid runs out into the first rain of the year. So the rain is welcomed with the skin, asked for with open hands, and redirected when it harms, with the same Lord addressed every time.
That's the puzzle solved: nobody in the story was asking God for weather. They were asking for benefit, and benefit sometimes means less.

how: When rain begins, many Muslims say the Prophet's words from al-Bukhari, sayyiban nafi'an (a beneficial rain); when rain does harm, some say his other words, around us, not on us.

o: a prayer asking God to hold back a coming storm
a short prayer asking for rain that does good
a thank-you said after the rain has stopped

games.q: the rain puzzle — tap the pairs.

s: when the rain did harm, the Prophet prayed for it to stop completely
he asked: around us, not on us. on the hills and valleys. the rain was moved, not canceled.
the Prophet once let the rain fall on him on purpose
in Sahih Muslim he uncovers part of his garment and says it has just come from its Lord.
the rain prayer simply asks God for more rain
it asks for a beneficial rain. the second word does the work.

games.q: your town's been in drought for months, and the forecast finally shows a huge storm with flood warnings. what fits the rain prayer best?
o: ask that it rain hard enough to end the drought, whatever it costs.
ask for the rain, and that it fall where it helps and not where it harms.
don't ask for anything; the weather isn't a thing to pray about.
games.why: a beneficial rain, and around us, not on us: the Prophet asked for rain, and asked for it to land where it does good.

practice: Find the nearest sound of water: rain on a window, a running tap, a kettle starting to hum. Listen to it for the whole sit, and let the two words ride on it if you like: sayyiban nafi'an.

wordCard.voice: When it rains. Muslims say sayyiban nafi'an, a beneficial rain: asking not for more weather, but for the kind that helps.

orig.note: Arabic: nafi', beneficial, useful. In the rain prayer: sayyiban nafi'an, a beneficial downpour.

carryVoice: The line for today: beneficial rain: not more of it, the good kind. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1032 (sayyiban nafi'an, on seeing rain)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1013–1014 (the Friday request for rain, and the next Friday's 'around us, not on us')
Sahih Muslim 898 (rain 'recently come from its Lord')
